source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"First-trimester exposure may increase cardiac-malformation risk, so prompt prescriber review is appropriate.","B":"First-trimester exposure causes Ebstein anomaly in most pregnancies, so the fetal outcome is predictable.","C":"First-trimester exposure has no recognized cardiac concern, so pregnancy review can wait until later.","D":"Lithium-related fetal concerns occur only near delivery, so first-trimester exposure needs no review."}}
source_row.rationale: Current labeling describes a historical first-trimester cardiovascular-malformation signal, especially Ebstein anomaly, while later data suggest any increased risk is likely small and are insufficient to establish a drug-associated risk. Option A communicates the risk without overstating certainty. B is excessive, while C and D deny the labeled concern.
source_row.source_detail: Use in Specific Populations §8.1 Pregnancy: early first-trimester reports suggested increased cardiovascular malformations, especially Ebstein anomaly; later studies suggest any increased cardiac-malformation risk is likely small and data are insufficient to establish a drug-associated risk. Current DailyMed lithium label, revised 10/2023; pregnancy section/currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, reversal, monitoring and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client taking lithium learns she is in the first trimester of pregnancy. Which teaching is most accurate?
